draft.title: AC induction motors
card: In an AC induction motor, alternating current in the fixed outer coils (the stator) makes a magnetic field that rotates around the inside of the motor.
This rotating field sweeps across the conductors of the rotor, the part that turns. The changing flux induces an emf and so a current in the rotor.
The rotor current sits in the magnetic field, so it feels a force. By Lenz's law, the rotor turns to follow the field and so reduce the relative motion between them.
No electrical supply is connected to the rotor, so the motor needs no brushes or commutator. These parts wear out, so an induction motor needs little upkeep.
draft.remember: The rotating field induces current in the rotor, and the rotor follows the field.

a.q: How does the rotor of an AC induction motor get its current?
opts: It is induced by the rotating magnetic field
It is carried in through brushes from the supply
It is passed in through a commutator
It comes from permanent magnets on the stator
a.why: The rotating field changes the flux through the rotor, so an emf and current are induced. Brushes are not needed, because the rotor has no electrical supply connected to it.
a.clue: Nothing is wired to the rotor.

b.q: A workshop in Wagga Wagga uses an AC induction motor to run a fan for many hours a day. Why does the motor need little upkeep?
opts: It has no brushes that wear away
It has no coils in the stator
It uses a commutator to reverse current
It needs no magnetic field to turn
b.why: The rotor current is induced, so no brushes touch the rotor and wear down. The stator does have coils, and the motor depends on a rotating magnetic field to turn.
b.clue: Think about which parts rub against each other and wear out.

a.best: It is induced by the rotating magnetic field

b.best: It has no brushes that wear away

check.summary: No problems found. The card matches the HSC treatment of the squirrel-cage induction motor, and both questions have one clear answer that the explanations support.
